title: VFX artist, junior

noc.title: Graphic arts technicians
noc.applies_when: What Job Bank maps "VFX Artist" to. The default for a compositing, roto, cleanup or general VFX seat.

noc.title: Other technical and coordinating occupations in motion pictures, broadcasting and performing arts
noc.applies_when: Lists "special effects technician" as an illustrative example. Fits on-set and practical-adjacent VFX work.

adjacent: post-production artist. Virtual production and real-time are where his Unreal work makes him unusually competitive and the postings are less contested than roto seats

skills.name: Compositing
skills.asked_for: Node-based compositing, the core discipline of the lane
skills.evidence: Nuke, plus the Fanshawe VFX programme. Lock-off compositing short film as a dedicated project.

skills.name: Nuke
skills.asked_for: The industry standard. Named in the large majority of postings
skills.evidence: Listed as a working tool; Fanshawe programme trained on it. Note: the lane 9 matrix understated this as "not yet" and has been corrected.

skills.name: Rotoscoping
skills.asked_for: Frame-accurate roto, the work junior VFX artists actually do all day
skills.evidence: Named project work: commercial edit using roto and object removal.

skills.name: Cleanup and paint
skills.asked_for: Removal, patching, rig removal
skills.evidence: Object removal and cleanup across student project work.

skills.name: Motion tracking
skills.asked_for: 2D tracking and match-moving
skills.evidence: Trailer sequence with motion tracking and object replacement.

skills.name: CG integration
skills.asked_for: Putting rendered elements into a plate so they sit
skills.evidence: Listed capability across After Effects, Nuke, Blender and Unreal.

skills.name: After Effects
skills.asked_for: The second tool, and the primary one for motion graphics seats
skills.evidence: Titles, lower thirds, transitions, plus VFX work.

skills.name: Colour and matching
skills.asked_for: Matching grade, grain and light between plate and element
skills.evidence: Grading experience through editing work. Plate matching specifically is programme-level rather than production-proven.
skills.limit: Plate matching specifically is programme-level rather than production-proven.

skills.name: Shot organisation and delivery
skills.asked_for: Versions, naming, delivery specs, working to a shot list
skills.evidence: Personal and client delivery discipline. Not a studio shot-tracking pipeline.

skills.name: Blender or Maya
skills.asked_for: 3D for modelling, lighting and rendering elements
skills.evidence: Blender listed as a working tool. Maya is the studio standard and is not evidenced.
skills.limit: Maya is the studio standard and is not evidenced.

skills.name: Unreal Engine for VFX
skills.asked_for: Virtual production, real-time rendering, LED volume work
skills.evidence: Active UE5 work across Death Bridge and the JKR channel. This is the differentiator in this lane, because real-time and virtual production is where VFX hiring is growing and few junior compositors have it.

skills.name: Python scripting
skills.asked_for: Nuke automation, pipeline tooling
skills.evidence: Strong Python generally, which transfers directly and is rare among junior VFX artists. Nuke-specific scripting is the small remaining step.

skills.name: Shot tracking software
skills.asked_for: ShotGrid, ftrack
skills.note: Studio-standard. Named in postings, learned on the job.

skills.name: On-set VFX supervision basics
skills.asked_for: Data wrangling, reference, HDRI capture
skills.evidence: Camera and on-set experience through his own shoots. Not on a VFX-supervised set.

skills.name: Houdini
skills.asked_for: FX simulation. Narrows the market when absent
skills.note: Only required for FX-specific seats, not for comp.

skills.name: Matchmove and 3D tracking
skills.asked_for: 3DEqualizer, SynthEyes

skills.name: Fusion
skills.asked_for: DaVinci's compositor, occasionally named

skills.name: Mocha
skills.asked_for: Planar tracking, common alongside Nuke

skills.name: Lighting and look development
skills.asked_for: A specialisation of its own

skills.name: FX simulation at production scale
skills.asked_for: Houdini territory

positioning:
Better supported than it looks. He has a recent named VFX credential, a live portfolio site, Nuke, and specific named project work across the exact tasks junior VFX roles hire for: roto, cleanup, object removal, motion tracking, object replacement, lock-off compositing. That is a real junior VFX profile, not an aspiration.

Two things make him unusual rather than typical. Unreal Engine plus VFX points straight at virtual production, which is the growth end of the industry. Python plus VFX points at pipeline and technical-artist work, which studios struggle to hire and which pays better than roto. Both are worth leading with over the standard "I can composite" framing, because the standard framing puts him in a queue behind everyone else with the same diploma.

The honest gaps are Maya, shot tracking software and studio pipeline experience, all of which are learned on the job and none of which should stop an application. Most in-scope postings grade Tier A or Tier B.

The reel is the application. In this lane more than any other, the portfolio decides the outcome and the resume barely matters. Breakdowns matter more than finished shots: show the plate, the roto, the elements and the comp, because that is what a VFX supervisor is actually reading for.
interview_watch: Expect a reel and breakdown review, and expect to be asked exactly what you did on each shot, because reels routinely overstate. Answer precisely and claim only your own work. Expect a question about handling notes and versions, which is really a question about whether you will be difficult in a review. Expect to be asked about turnaround and volume, since junior comp work is measured in shots per week. For virtual production and technical-artist seats, lead with Unreal and Python and let the compositing be the supporting evidence.
pr_note: All three candidate codes are TEER 2 and clear the floor, so this lane is PR-worthy but sits a tier below lane 11. No RCIP community list covers any of them, so never tag a lane 12 role RCIP. AIP covers the lane from a designated Atlantic employer with no occupation list, and Ontario's Workforce Priority stream takes any NOC with a qualifying offer, which matters because the Ontario VFX market is where the jobs are.
not_required: Feature credits, union membership, or a degree beyond the Fanshawe programme. A posting requiring shipped feature credits has failed the seniority gate.

notes.heading: Intro
notes.text: New in v3.5. NOC 52111, 52119 or 52120, all TEER 2. Read 00-index.md for the Status conventions and tier rules.

notes.heading: Credentials
notes.text: - Visual Effects and Editing for Contemporary Media, Fanshawe College, London ON (2024 to 2025). A named VFX credential, recently completed. This is a real differentiator: most junior VFX applicants are self-taught and this lane still respects programme training. - Portfolio site: film.kkvasan.ca, already built and live, with categories and video embeds.

notes.heading: Sourcing notes
notes.text:
Geography reality: Canadian VFX concentrates in Vancouver and Toronto, with Montreal third and usually French-gated. Toronto is the realistic target from London for hybrid or onsite, Vancouver for remote or relocation. Remote junior VFX is rare because studios run security-controlled pipelines, so expect onsite or hybrid requirements and treat a fully-remote junior comp posting with some suspicion.

Studio names worth watching directly in an employer-first pass: the major Vancouver and Toronto facilities post on their own careers pages more reliably than they appear on aggregators.
